q: What is the primary reason most of the world's vines are grafted onto American rootstock?
opts: To reduce the need for pruning
exp: American Vitis species evolved alongside phylloxera and tolerate its root feeding. Grafting vinifera onto that rootstock is the durable answer to the louse.

q: In the vine, what is the main function of the leaf canopy?
exp: Leaves convert sunlight into the sugars that ripen the fruit. Canopy management is largely about giving leaves useful light without shading the fruit.

q: What term describes a vine shoot in its woody, mature state after the growing season?
exp: A green shoot lignifies into a cane over the season. The distinction matters at pruning, where the choice is between retaining canes or short spurs.

q: Which part of the grape contributes the greatest share of tannin?
exp: Tannin sits mainly in skins and seeds, with stems adding more if included. Pulp is largely water, sugar and acid, which is why most grapes give pale juice.

q: What is the correct order of the vine's growing season?
opts: Budbreak, flowering, fruit set, veraison, harvest
Budbreak, veraison, flowering, fruit set, harvest
Fruit set, flowering, budbreak, veraison, harvest
Flowering, budbreak, veraison, fruit set, harvest
exp: Dormancy gives way to budbreak, then flowering, then fruit set, then veraison, then harvest. Veraison is the turn from growth into ripening.

q: In the Southern Hemisphere, harvest typically falls in which months?
exp: The seasons invert, putting Southern Hemisphere harvest around February to April against the Northern Hemisphere's late summer into autumn.

q: Poor weather during flowering that causes flowers to fail and drop is known as what?
exp: Coulure is failure of fruit set, leaving a sparse bunch. Millerandage is the related disorder producing bunches of uneven, seedless small berries.

q: During dormancy, what is the vine doing?
opts: Ripening the last of its fruit
Pushing new shoots out of its buds
Producing a second crop from lateral shoots
exp: The vine drops its leaves and rests through winter. Cold winters that enforce true dormancy are part of why many classic regions sit where they do.

q: What is the significance of fruit set?
opts: It is when the wine is pressed
It sets the potential crop size
It is when the vine is grafted
It marks the end of ripening
exp: Fruit set is where fertilised flowers become berries, so it effectively fixes how many berries the vine will carry. Bad weather here costs the whole vintage's volume.

q: Which climate type is defined by a large difference between summer and winter temperatures?
exp: Continental climates swing hard between hot summers and cold winters, and the growing season is short. Maritime climates are moderated by water and vary far less.

q: A Mediterranean climate is best characterised by which pattern?
opts: Cool wet summers and dry winters
Warm dry summers and mild wet winters
Extreme day-to-night swings in the winter
exp: Warm, dry summers with rainfall concentrated in the mild winter is the Mediterranean signature. It suits ripening but often makes water the limiting factor.

q: What does a large diurnal temperature shift preserve in ripening grapes?
exp: Cold nights slow the respiration that burns off acid, so fruit can reach ripeness while retaining freshness. It is why altitude and cool nights are prized in warm regions.

q: Between which approximate latitudes does most of the world's viticulture sit?
exp: The classic bands run roughly 30 to 50 degrees in both hemispheres, where the growing season is warm enough to ripen fruit but cool enough to keep balance.

q: Why is spring frost so damaging?
opts: It kills the newly burst buds and shoots that carry the crop
It freezes the sap in the trunk, splitting the wood permanently
It kills the vine's roots outright, so the vine must be replanted
It causes grey rot in ripe fruit
exp: Frost after budbreak kills the tender buds and green shoots that would have borne fruit. Secondary buds may push but usually yield less and ripen later.

q: Which frost protection method works by releasing heat as water freezes on the vine?
exp: Water gives up latent heat as it freezes, holding the bud at around zero under a shell of ice. Wind machines instead mix warmer air down from above the inversion layer.

q: Rain immediately before harvest most directly risks which two problems?
exp: Vines take up the water, swelling berries and diluting concentration, while damp bunches invite grey rot. It is the classic reason to pick before a forecast front.
